The second bottle came three days after the first, carried in on a gentle morning tide. Elias found it at sunrise, nestled in a bed of bladderwrack as if placed there by hand. Same glass, same red wax seal.

"October 19th — the old pier at Harrowby will collapse during the school trip. A child will fall through. She will not surface unless someone enters the water from the east stairs."

Elias didn't laugh this time.

He spent October 18th pacing the lighthouse gallery, arguing with himself. It was coincidence. It had to be coincidence. The Mary Ellen was old, everyone knew she'd capsize eventually. But the date, the name, the location — those weren't coincidence. Those were precision.

At nine in the morning on October 19th, Elias stationed himself at the east stairs of the old pier. He told himself he was being ridiculous. He told himself that right up until the timber cracked and a girl in a red coat plunged through the gap.

He was in the water before the scream finished echoing off the harbor wall. The cold hit like concrete. He found the girl tangled in submerged netting, pulled her free, and kicked for the surface. Hands reached down from the pier and hauled them both out.

By afternoon, Elias Mercer was the talk of Harrowby. The reclusive lighthouse keeper who'd saved little Rosie Calder. The harbor master, a broad man called Tom Vane, shook his hand so hard Elias thought his shoulder would dislocate.

"How'd you know to be there?" Tom asked, eyes narrowing.

"Luck," Elias said. The word tasted like rust.

The third bottle arrived the next morning. This one stopped his breath:

"October 31st — Harvest Festival night. Fire in the town hall. Starts in the kitchen store cupboard. Seventeen people inside. The doors jam."

Elias went to Tom Vane first. He sat in the harbor master's office and explained — the bottles, the predictions, all of it. Tom listened, then rubbed his face with both hands.

"Elias, you've been alone up in that tower too long."

He tried the constable next, then the pub landlord. Same answer each time, delivered with varying degrees of pity. The crazy lighthouse keeper and his messages from the sea.

It was Tom's daughter who found him sitting on the harbor wall that evening, staring at the note. Marina Vane was twenty-six, sharp-featured, practical. She ran the marine supply shop and had no patience for nonsense.

"My father says you've lost it," she said, sitting down beside him.

"Your father might be right."

She held out her hand. "Show me the note."

He handed it over. She read it, turned it over, held it up to the fading light. Then she looked at him — really looked — and said, "The handwriting's the same on all three?"

"Identical."

Marina folded the note carefully and handed it back. "I don't believe in prophecy," she said. "But I believe in patterns. And you've got a pattern. So what's the plan for the town hall?"
